sections.title: The Bride's Preparations
sections.html:
Ahead of the wedding, the bride needs to learn the fundamentals of the mitzva of simḥat ona (the mitzva of marital joy and intimacy) and the laws of purity, and it is good to learn them with the help of a madrikhat kallot (bridal instructor). As in every field, there are better instructors and less good ones. The sign of a good instructor is that she is well versed in the halakhot and knows how to explain them well, and she expands on explaining the mitzva of simḥat ona and its value (as explained in Peninei Halakha: Simḥat Ha-bayit U-virkhato, chapters 1-3), and from there proceeds to explain the laws of tum'a and tahara (impurity and purity), which are meant to direct, elevate and intensify love and joy. But a less good instructor turns things upside down; she does not base her instruction on the essence of the mitzva, which is the complete union, and she does not explain the halakhot well either.

Nearly all brides today customarily make use of hormonal pills to regulate the timing of the last veset (menstrual period) before the wedding, so that it falls at a time that allows the bride to become pure in time for the wedding, and yet falls at least three weeks before the wedding, so that immediately after the bride becomes impure from dam betulim (hymenal blood) and stops taking the pills, the next veset will arrive, and the period of impurity will be shortened. One should know that there are different pills, and each of them suits most women, while in some women it causes slight bleeding between cycles or low mood. Therefore, the bride should consult a doctor who is familiar with the subject early enough to be able to take the pills for two cycles before the wedding, so that if she sees that the pills do not suit her, the doctor can change the type of pill or its dosage, and the bride will arrive at her wedding pure and calm.

sections.title: Taking Care to Avoid a Ḥuppat Nidda
sections.html:
The bride must make every possible effort to arrive at the wedding when she is pure. For otherwise the joy of the wedding will be greatly harmed, and the groom and bride will have to observe all the laws of harḥakot (distancing measures) that we learned above (in chapter 3). This includes that they will be forbidden to touch hands and to pass an object from one to the other. However, at the time of the ḥuppa, in order to prevent embarrassment, the groom will be permitted to cover the bride with the veil, to place the ring on her finger, and to give her the cup of wine and the ketuba, while trying not to touch her. In addition, until the bride becomes pure, the prohibition of yiḥud (seclusion) applies to them, and they will have to sleep in separate rooms in their parents' home, or in another house where other people are present (as explained below, section 13). Likewise, after the ḥuppa they will be forbidden to be secluded in the "yiḥud room."1

In addition, some say that the marriage depends on the groom and bride being secluded in complete seclusion that is fit for the mitzva of ona (marital relations), and when the bride is not pure they are forbidden to be secluded, and consequently the marriage does not take effect (Rambam). However, since postponing the wedding would cause great losses and distress, the custom is to follow the opinion of most poskim, and the wedding is held even when the bride is not pure – a ḥuppat nidda (a wedding held while the bride is nidda, in a state of menstrual impurity).2

sections.title: Bedikot for a Virgin Bride
sections.html:
Ahead of her wedding the bride must become pure from her veset blood, and also from the concern of dam ḥimud ("blood of desire"), as we will learn in the next section. To begin the process of purification she must perform the bedika (internal examination) of hefsek tahara (the examination establishing that bleeding has ceased) at least eight days before the wedding. After that, when the sun sets, she begins counting the shiv'a neki'im (seven clean days). During the shiv'a neki'im the bride should examine herself twice every day, once in the morning and once before sunset. If this is difficult for her, she may examine herself once each day. If she forgot and examined herself only twice during the seven days, she has fulfilled the obligation of the bedikot (as explained above, 4:8).

The bedikot of hefsek tahara and of the shiv'a neki'im are carried out with a white cloth called an ed bedika (examination cloth), and they are meant to verify that there is no bleeding from the uterus (above, 4:2). Ordinarily these bedikot must be performed deep within the vagina and "in the holes and crevices," that is, on all sides of the vagina (above, 4:3). However, because of the hymen, the bride cannot examine inside the vagina but only at its opening, without causing the slightest pain, so that no blood comes out from the hymen.

The seven days end exactly one week after the hefsek: if the hefsek tahara was performed toward the end of Tuesday, and she began the shiv'a neki'im on the night of Wednesday (Tuesday night), then the following week too the shiv'a neki'im will end at the end of Tuesday, and immediately after tzeit ha-kokhavim (nightfall) on Tuesday night she may perform tevila (immersion).3

sections.title: Purification from Dam Ḥimud
sections.html:
The Sages instituted that when a bride agrees to marry, she counts shiv'a neki'im and immerses. For perhaps, out of the realization that she is about to marry and to unite with her groom in complete union, her heart will go out to him in desire, and out of her excitement dam ḥimud will come out of her uterus and she will become impure from it (Nidda 66a). And even if she examined herself and did not see blood, it is possible that a little blood came out and was lost in the natural moisture found in the vagina. The time at which there is concern for dam ḥimud is the time of agreeing to marry, for then the bride becomes clearly aware that she is about to marry. If the agreement to marry was given long before the wedding, the time when there is a chance that she will see dam ḥimud is when the final preparations begin, about two or three weeks before the wedding.

Even a woman who does not menstruate, such as an older woman who has stopped seeing menstrual blood, since she received a marriage proposal and agreed, may become excited and see dam ḥimud, and she must count shiv'a neki'im and immerse ahead of her wedding (Nidda 66a). And although most likely she did not see blood, since the Sages instituted that a bride counts shiv'a neki'im and immerses ahead of her wedding, she must recite a blessing over the tevila.

A bride who is able to become pure from her last veset a week or two before the wedding should preferably postpone the shiv'a neki'im so that she immerses a day or two before her wedding, and at most four days before the wedding. For some say that the closer the wedding date approaches, the greater the chance that she will become excited and dam ḥimud will come out, and it is therefore good for her to bring her purifying tevila close to the date of her wedding. In addition, it is good that even after her tevila she examines herself every day until her wedding day with an external wiping examination, to make sure that she has not begun to see blood due to desire.4

If the bride immersed and became pure ahead of the wedding, and a quarrel broke out and they called off the wedding, and then they again agreed to marry, she must again count shiv'a neki'im and immerse, lest at the time the marriage was decided anew she saw dam ḥimud (SA YD 192:3).

Likewise, when a man takes back his divorced wife, even if she is pregnant by him, she must count shiv'a neki'im and become pure from the concern of dam ḥimud (SA YD 192:5; Radbaz 3:423; Torat Ha-shelamim 9).

Even when elderly people marry, the bride must count shiv'a neki'im and become pure. But if it is clear that the groom's virility has already ceased, and the purpose of the marriage is companionship and help, she need not be concerned about dam ḥimud or count shiv'a neki'im.5

sections.title: A Spiritual Reason for Not Meeting in the Week Before the Wedding
sections.html:
According to the rules of halakha and the safeguards that the Sages set in the laws of ketamim (bloodstains), the law should have been that only if the bride actually sees blood due to desire does she become impure, but if in practice she sees no blood other than her regular menstrual blood, she need not be concerned about additional blood of desire. However, the Sages were more stringent in this law, and were concerned that dam ḥimud may have come out and she did not see it because it was lost, and they therefore instituted that every bride must become pure from the concern of dam ḥimud. It seems that the Sages also had a spiritual reason: that every bride should purify herself, ahead of her wedding, from the period of wondering and searching, in which she had not yet merited to complete herself in a partnership and could only desire and long. And she should sanctify herself through shiv'a neki'im and tevila ahead of her union with her husband in love and joy. The counting of these days is like the counting of the seven weeks that Israel counted toward the giving of the Torah, which is considered the "wedding day" between the Holy One, blessed be He, and Knesset Yisrael (the Congregation of Israel).

Following on from this, in recent generations a fine custom has spread among Israel that the groom and bride do not meet during the week leading up to the wedding, and many also try not to speak on the phone. It seems that the halakhic basis for this is in the words of the Rishonim who hold that the closer the date of the wedding approaches while they still cannot marry, the more the concern of dam ḥimud may increase, and if they meet there is greater reason for this concern. The spiritual reason for the custom is that during this special week, out of longing and yearning for the joy of marriage, they purify themselves from the period in which they were lacking and could only desire and long, and they sanctify themselves ahead of their marriage in joy and love.6

sections.title: Teshuva Ahead of the Wedding
sections.html:
It is a mitzva for the groom and bride to be aroused to teshuva (repentance) ahead of their wedding, and especially on their wedding day, and to pray to God that they merit to live together in love and joy, and merit to engage in Torah and mitzvot, and to help each other realize all their talents and fulfil all their good aspirations, for the glory of the Torah and the building of the nation and the land. And that they merit to honour their parents, and to have children and raise them to Torah, to mitzvot, to the ḥuppa and to good deeds. And that they merit good health and a good livelihood. And that they merit to observe Shabbatot and festivals with joy and contentment. And it is good for them to pray also for their family members and friends.

The Sages said (Yevamot 63b): "Once a man marries a woman, his sins are stopped up (sealed), as it is stated (Mishlei 18:22): 'He who finds a wife finds good, and obtains favour from the Lord.'" The bride too merits this on her wedding day, for everything the Sages said about the groom applies also to the bride. The reason their sins are forgiven is that while they are single they are like two halves that have not found their completion, as the Sages said (Yevamot 63a): "Any man who has no wife is not a man." And they still dwell without joy, without blessing, without goodness, without Torah, without a wall, without peace (ibid. 62b). By marrying in faith and love according to the law of Moshe and Israel, they unite and complete themselves and are like someone born anew, and their sins, which had influenced their character for the worse, are hidden away and stopped up. If they merit to return in complete teshuva, their sins will be transformed into merits, and together with all their good inclinations they will grow and flourish, deepening and enlarging their love and enriching their lives. But if they return to sin, the sins will return to their place, and the bad inclinations and aspects of their character will spring up like thorns and embitter their lives.

On Yom Kippur we make great efforts to return in teshuva sincerely and honestly, whereas on the wedding day, because of the great holiness of the occasion, the groom and bride can merit this without special efforts. For they truly want to live from now on in faith and love, to build a good family and to do good deeds. Therefore their teshuva is accepted on this day in a special way, and consequently their prayers are answered.

sections.title: The Custom of Fasting on the Wedding Day
sections.html:
In most communities of Israel the custom is that grooms and brides fast on their wedding day, in order to purify and refine themselves through teshuva, and out of this to pray to God that He grant them, in His abundant kindness, to fulfil all their good aspirations. In addition, there was a concern that out of tension and pressure some grooms would eat and drink excessively and would not come to the ḥuppa with the proper seriousness, and perhaps would not even be focused because of drinking alcoholic beverages. There are communities of Sephardic and Eastern origin in which the custom was not to fast on the wedding day, and there are communities in which the custom was that grooms fast and brides do not, and the brides' teshuva was accomplished through their tevila ahead of the wedding. In practice, it is proper for every groom to follow the custom of his father and every bride that of her mother. And ba'alei teshuva (those who have returned to observance) should choose the custom that seems good to them.

Even in families whose custom is to fast, one does not fast on days on which it is forbidden to fast, such as Rosh Ḥodesh, Ḥanukka and the month of Nisan. A groom or bride who fears that the fast will weaken them or give them headaches is not obligated to fast. Admittedly, in the past only a few were lenient in this, but today, after we have grown accustomed to lives of plenty and comfort, fasts have become more difficult emotionally, and therefore when the fast causes distress we are lenient, since this fast is meant to arouse teshuva and not to bring atonement and refinement through accepting suffering. We find the same with regard to other fasts: in the past many used to fast on them for atonement and refinement through accepting suffering, whereas today the accepted guidance is to increase charity, Torah study and teshuva instead of fasting. Therefore, those who are concerned about the fast are not obligated to fast; they should eat and drink as they need, refrain from alcoholic drink, and arouse themselves to teshuva by setting a time for Torah study on the wedding day and by giving charity. And if they are able, it is better that they fast until midday.

The custom of fasting continues until after the ḥuppa or until tzeit ha-kokhavim, whichever comes first (Ḥokhmat Adam 129:2; Sedei Ḥemed, Ma'arekhet Ḥatan Ve-kalla 4).7

sections.title: Be'ilat Mitzva
sections.html:
There is a special virtue in the first union, which is also called be'ilat mitzva (the mitzva union), in which the groom and bride unite in complete union and make an eternal covenant between them. As Adam said after he met his wife and married her: "And the man said: This one at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man. Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and cling to his wife, and they shall become one flesh" (Bereishit 2:23-24). Through this they will be able to continue to express their unity in the mitzva of ona, in love and joy, all the days of their lives. And through this they will also merit to fulfil the mitzva of peru u-revu (being fruitful and multiplying) (Tosafot Ketubot 4a).

The betulim (virginity) express the bride's guarding of herself for her husband, so that he will open the wellspring of life within her, and out of pleasure and joy she will merit to bear him sons and daughters. In this union that opens the betulim there is pleasure, and sometimes also pain, which expresses the covenant that the groom and bride make between them – a covenant that will endure always, for better and for worse. As it is stated (Yeḥezkel 16:6): "And I passed by you and saw you wallowing in your blood, and I said to you: In your blood, live; and I said to you: In your blood, live." That is to say, although the world is full of imperfections, and the groom and bride too are not perfect, the bride's readiness to open herself to her groom so that they can unite, and the groom's readiness to commit himself to caring for her happiness, cover over every deficiency. Thereby an eternal covenant is made between them, through whose fulfilment they will merit to continue their shared life forever – in this world through their descendants, and in the World to Come through the union of their souls.8

sections.title: Virginity in the Past and Today
sections.html:
The ketuba that the Sages instituted is meant to secure the bride's rights, and at its centre is the sum she will receive should the marriage come to an end, through divorce or the husband's death. Regarding the amount of the ketuba, the Sages instituted that one who marries a betula (virgin), since he merits to know that he is her only one, obligates himself for at least two hundred zuz, and one who marries a bride who is not a virgin obligates himself for at least one hundred zuz (Ketubot 10b). In the past, if no blood came out after the be'ilat mitzva, it became clear that the bride had not been a virgin, and the groom could claim that since he had married her on the assumption that she was a virgin, the marriage should be annulled, or the sum of the ketuba reduced. But today, when no blood is found after the be'ilat mitzva, it is not possible to make this claim, for since the bride is older, over the age of eighteen, sometimes the hymen naturally stretches by itself and the opening opens, and no blood comes out as a result of the union. The older the bride, the greater the chance that no blood will come out at the first union, and if the bride was also accustomed to using a tampon during her period, most likely the hymen has stretched and she will not see blood.9

Although, as a result of the later age of marriage, the hymen is often already stretched and does not break at the be'ilat mitzva, the virtue of be'ilat mitzva still remains in place, for through it the groom and bride unite and make an eternal covenant.10

sections.title: Dam Betulim and Its Impurity
sections.html:
The Sages instituted that after the groom is secluded with his virgin bride and they have performed the be'ilat mitzva completely, the bride becomes impure on account of the dam betulim. But the groom need not hurry to withdraw after his seed has come out; rather, they are permitted to continue embracing in the position of union. When they decide to part, the groom withdraws from the bride and they begin to observe all the harḥakot of the days of nidda.

Admittedly, by Torah law dam betulim is considered dam makka, that is, blood of a wound, which does not render impure. However, the Sages were concerned that out of the excitement of the breaking of the hymen, blood that does render impure might come out of the uterus together with the hymenal blood. It seems that the Sages were also concerned that if they were lenient about dam betulim, the hymenal bleeding might continue in the subsequent unions as well, since these take place in succession without time for the wound to heal, and then, even when the veset begins, there would be those who would mistakenly think it is dam betulim and would transgress a prohibition punishable by karet. This is especially so in the days after the wedding, when the desire of the groom and bride intensifies, and if they do not make a safeguard and treat all blood as forbidden, they may come to a prohibition.11

Even if after the union the bride did not see dam betulim, they must separate as with a nidda, for since she was a virgin, perhaps a little blood came out of her and was lost, or semen covered it. This is on condition that both of them are sure that there was a complete union, in such a way that the entire organ entered the vagina and the seed came out. But if they are in doubt about this: if they saw blood on the sheet or on the cloth with which they wiped themselves, she has become impure, and if they did not see blood, she is pure. Only after they have had a complete union does she become impure even if they did not see blood, lest blood came out and they did not see it. To avoid the doubt, it is preferable that they use a dark sheet and cloths on which blood is not seen, and then, if they are in doubt whether there was a complete union, they will not need to separate.12

A bride who is not a virgin, such as a widow or a divorcee, or even a single woman who has already had marital relations not in holiness, does not become impure at the first union, since she has no dam betulim.

sections.title: The Bride's Purification After Dam Betulim
sections.html:
After the groom and bride separate from each other, she cannot immediately begin counting shiv'a neki'im, since we learned (above, 4:5-7) that as long as semen may come out of the vagina, a woman cannot begin to become pure. And since for three full days the semen may still come out, she should wait until the fourth day from the union and toward its end perform the hefsek tahara, and then begin the shiv'a neki'im. If she wishes, on the day after the union she may thoroughly wipe the vagina to clean it of all remnants of semen, and on that same day, before sunset, perform the hefsek tahara and begin counting shiv'a neki'im.13

In practice, however, the widespread custom is that the bride takes pills to postpone the veset, and immediately after the complete union she stops taking them, and within a few days she gets her veset, and then only after the veset blood ends can she perform the hefsek tahara and begin counting shiv'a neki'im.

If, after the bride has become pure and they have had union, she again sees blood from her hymen, she becomes impure again, and so too a third time, for as long as remnants of her hymen remain and she sees blood from them, she becomes impure. The distress this causes is very great; therefore everything should be done to prevent repeated impurity from dam betulim. The advice for this is that on the day after the be'ilat mitzva in which the bride became impure from dam betulim, she should feel the area of the hymen with a damp cloth in order to remove the remnants of the hymen (as explained in the note). Experience shows that after this procedure the chance that she will see blood again is very low. Then, if she nevertheless sees blood on days on which she is not expected to get her veset, this blood will no longer be considered dam betulim, which renders impure, but rather blood that came out of a wound formed on the sides of the vagina as a result of the removal of the hymen, which does not render impure.14

sections.title: Removing the Hymen by a Medical Procedure
sections.html:
When union is too painful, and after several attempts the groom and bride realize that they are not succeeding in breaking the hymen, because it is particularly thick or because they are particularly apprehensive, they should go to a doctor who will open the hymen with a minor surgical procedure. According to halakha, even though blood comes out from this procedure, the bride does not become impure. For the Sages' enactment is that the bride becomes impure from dam betulim that came out during union, lest, out of the arousal that accompanies union with the groom, veset blood or dam ḥimud also come out of her uterus; but when the hymen was opened by a medical procedure there is no such concern. Afterwards, even if the bride sees blood following union, it will be dam makka, which does not render impure, since it came out from the wound left in the vagina and not from the hymen itself.

Likewise, a woman who did not succeed in carrying out the advice mentioned in the previous section may go to a doctor who will check whether her hymen has opened completely, and if the doctor sees that part of it still obstructs the opening, she will open what remains. Then, if the next time the bride sees blood after union, this blood will be considered blood of a wound, and she will not become impure from it.15

sections.title: When the Prohibition of Yiḥud Applies
sections.html:
As a rule, a man and a woman who are forbidden to each other may not be alone in a place where they cannot be seen, lest they come to sin. This prohibition is called the prohibition of yiḥud. Seemingly, a husband and his wife during her nidda period should also be forbidden to be alone in their home, but since they have already merited to rejoice together in the mitzva of ona, and will again merit to fulfil the mitzva of ona after she becomes pure, they have the strength to overcome their inclination and wait until she becomes pure. We have already learned (above, 3:1) that the Talmud relates (Sanhedrin 37a) that a Christian priest asked Rav Kahana: You say that a man is permitted to be in a closed house with his wife when she is a nidda – "is it possible for fire to be in flax and not singe it?!" Can young people overcome their inclination and not sin?! He answered him: "The Torah testified about us, 'hedged about with roses' – that even with a hedge (a fence and boundary) of roses, they will not breach it." That is, the safeguards of distancing that the Sages instituted, which are like a soft fence of roses, keep the couple from sin. And this is on condition that they have already had union once.

But if there was a ḥuppat nidda, or if the wife saw a veset and became impure before they managed to have union, they are forbidden in yiḥud until she immerses and becomes pure and they have union.

Even if they lay together in kiruv basar (skin-to-skin contact) without any barrier between them, not even underwear, the prohibition of yiḥud no longer applies to them. But if out of excessive apprehension one of the spouses shied away from skin-to-skin contact without any barrier, and the bride saw a veset, they are forbidden in yiḥud.16

The convenient advice for a groom and bride who are forbidden in yiḥud is that after the wedding they go to the home of the groom's or the bride's parents and live with them until the night of the tevila. During that time the groom and bride should sleep in two separate rooms between which one cannot pass without going through the hallway in which the parents or other members of the household walk (see Ketubot 4a; SA YD 192:4). And when they are not sleeping, they should be careful not to be alone in a closed room; during the day the main thing to be careful about is that the room not be locked, so that the members of the household can enter at any moment. In the evening they must be more careful, that the door be open and the room lit. If the groom and bride want to be in their own home, the way to prevent yiḥud is for them to host in their home two children from their family aged about six or over, so that at night the groom sleeps with the boy in one room and the bride with the girl in another room.

sections.title: Postponing Be'ilat Mitzva
sections.html:
As is the way of the world, grooms and brides want to rejoice together with the joy of a mitzva throughout the seven days of celebration, and are very distressed that the bride becomes impure immediately after the first night because of dam betulim. In addition, many find it difficult to move from a stage in which touching is forbidden to fulfilling the mitzva in the proper manner, which may cause the first union to involve unpleasantness. And if they do not have the chance to get to know each other and give each other joy, the memory of the first days after the wedding, which are supposed to be especially joyful, may be a sad one. In addition, if the bride does not have the chance to experience pleasure, and only a painful experience remains with her from the first union, there is a concern that she will find it hard to free herself from the negative memory and open herself to fulfilling the mitzva of ona with joy.

Therefore, the proper advice is to postpone the be'ilat mitzva to the end of the seven days of celebration, and in the meantime they should give each other joy with great love. And since by nature, when the groom and bride give each other joy, it is very difficult for the groom to restrain himself from emitting his seed, when the groom feels his desire intensifying they should have union by light contact of the organ at the area of the opening of the vagina, in such a way that his seed goes out toward her without the slightest pressure on the hymen.

Some say, however, that it is preferable to hasten and perform the be'ilat mitzva as soon as possible, even though immediately afterwards the bride becomes impure and the couple must separate from each other. In their view, postponing the complete union even involves certain concerns, as cited in the note. Many follow their practice. However, it seems from experience that the correct guidance for our day is to postpone the be'ilat mitzva so that the groom and bride increase the joy of their love.17

sections.title: Be'ilat Mitzva on Shabbat
sections.html: It is permitted to perform the be'ilat mitzva on Shabbat. It is not to be forbidden on the grounds that one may not do distressing things on Shabbat, since the joy of the mitzva of union outweighs the distress of the breaking of the hymen. Nor is it to be forbidden because of the prohibition of ḥovel (wounding) on Shabbat, according to which it is forbidden to make a wound that draws blood out of the body, because the hymenal blood is considered as gathered and kept in its place in order to guard her opening, and breaking the hymen is not considered making a wound that causes blood to be drawn out of the body in general. Nor is it considered the melakha of improving something by making an opening, because in truth the state of the hymen is considered the more "improved" one, and breaking the hymen is considered spoiling it, which it is fitting to forgo only because of the great virtue of the union between the spouses (Ketubot 5b-7a; SA OḤ 280:2).

sections.title: Bedikot After the Wedding
sections.html:
Some say that a bride who does not have a fixed veset must verify that union does not cause her veset to appear. For this purpose, once it is clear that the dam betulim has stopped, during the first three times that they have union the groom and bride should examine themselves. This is how they do it: they prepare clean white cloths for examination; before union the bride examines herself to confirm that she is clean, so that she can be sure that her veset has not begun. After union the groom and bride examine themselves with the cloth, to verify that there is no blood on them as a result of the union. After they have examined themselves three times in this way, they will know with certainty that union does not cause the bride's veset to appear (SA YD 186:2, based on Rif, and many Aḥaronim).

In contrast, some say that there is no need to perform these bedikot, because according to most Rishonim there is no reason to be concerned, without cause, that union will bring on the veset (Rashi, Tosafot, Razah, Ritva and others). In practice too, the concern that union will bring on the veset is negligible. This was the practice in several communities (Shakh 186:1).

In practice, the halakha follows the lenient view, that there is no need to perform additional bedikot after the dam betulim has ended. Those who wish to be scrupulous may follow the stringent view.18
